analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 40% excess profits tax on oil companies for three years.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it died in the House Ways and Means Committee with no cosponsors, six weeks before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a 40% tax on the portion of an oil company's income that exceeds its normal earnings, applied for three years after enactment. Companies could reduce the tax by deducting what they reinvest in domestic drilling, pipelines, refining, and enhanced oil recovery. It was introduced in October 1990, referred to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee, and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers generally, since the revenue would flow to the Treasury; the implicit aim was to recapture windfall earnings oil companies picked up when prices spiked, rather than letting those earnings sit with the industry. It would not directly lower anyone's gas or heating-oil bill.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 40% tax on each oil corporation's income above a deduction equal to either its average 1986-1988 taxable income or a return on invested capital, whichever is greater [S3].
Applies for a three-year 'emergency period' beginning on enactment, on top of regular corporate income tax [S3].

Lets companies escape the tax on money plowed back into domestic production — intangible drilling costs, refineries, pipelines, and secondary or tertiary oil recovery — capped at 25% of excess profits income [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations producing crude oil, gasoline, fuel oil, and home heating oil in the United States, which would owe the extra 40% on profits above their base-period earnings; some of the cost could be passed through to consumers at the pump.

drawbacks.text: The base period (1986-1988) was a time of unusually low oil prices, so the bill could tax profits that were normal for the industry rather than genuinely windfall gains [S3].

Windfall profits taxes on oil can discourage investment in domestic production; the bill tries to blunt this with its energy plowback deduction, but the deduction is capped at 25% of excess profits income, so the incentive problem is only partly addressed [S3].
The revenue would go to the Treasury generally, not to consumers facing higher energy bills, so households hit by price spikes would not see direct relief from this tax [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a targeted effort to claw back a slice of oil-industry windfall earnings during a price spike, with a reasonable design feature — taxing only income above base-period earnings and rewarding reinvestment in domestic production. The revenue would help taxpayers broadly but would do nothing directly for consumers paying higher energy prices, and taxing against a low-price base period risks reaching normal profits, not just windfalls. It was never debated, so no committee weighed these trade-offs.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended; no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Benjamin Gilman introduced the bill on October 17, 1990 [S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which writes tax legislation [S5].
The action history shows no further action of any kind before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil companies producing petroleum in the United States are better off: no excess profits tax was ever enacted, and the windfall earnings the bill targeted were never taxed. The Ways and Means Committee never had to take a position.

for.name: Rep. Benjamin A. Gilman
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the excess profits tax bill and referred it to Ways and Means.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — so the bill died in committee.

against.name: Rep. Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration during the remaining weeks of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only supporter was a Republican, and it drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern ever formed; the decisive inaction was by the Democratic-chaired tax committee.

industries.note: The bill would have taken 40% of their profits above base-period earnings for three years, sparing only reinvested domestic drilling and production spending. Their interest in the bill ran against taxpayers, since the untaxed windfall stayed with the industry.

The energy plowback deduction would have made it cheaper for oil companies to reinvest in drilling, pipelines, refineries, and enhanced recovery, since every dollar spent there reduced the tax. That spend never happened because the bill died.
